title: Privacy-Preserving KYC: What Financial Institutions Should Know
summary: KYC does not inherently require collecting and storing all customer identity data. Privacy-preserving approaches can satisfy compliance while reducing data retention risk.
body_markdown:
KYC does not require collecting and storing everything. The Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and the Customer Identification Program (CIP) rules that implement it define specific obligations: verify that a customer is who they claim to be, assess risk, and maintain records sufficient to support examinations and law enforcement requests. Those requirements can be satisfied through multiple technical approaches. The approach most institutions use today, collecting and retaining raw copies of government-issued identity documents, is one option. It is not the only option, and it may not be the most defensible one from a risk perspective.


Privacy-preserving KYC uses verifiable digital credentials, selective disclosure, and in some configurations zero-knowledge proofs to answer compliance questions without accumulating personal data beyond what a compliance obligation actually requires. This article explains what that looks like, why it matters to compliance and security teams, and where the genuine complexity lies.


## What KYC Actually Requires


The CIP rule, codified at[31 CFR 1020.220](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-31/subtitle-B/chapter-X/part-1020/subpart-B/section-1020.220?ref=blog.spruceid.com) , requires banks with anti-money laundering compliance programs to implement a written Customer Identification Program that, at minimum, collects specific identifying information at account opening: name, date of birth, address, and an identification number. It requires verification of that information through documentary or non-documentary methods. And it requires retention of records describing the verification method and result.


The rule does not specify that an institution must store a copy of the underlying document indefinitely. It does not require maintaining a central repository of customer identity data beyond what is needed to document the verification decision. The retention requirements govern records of the verification, not necessarily the full document set used to perform it.


This distinction matters because many institutions have treated compliance as a floor and built data collection practices well above it, keeping full document scans, enriched consumer data, and other identity artifacts that compound liability without corresponding compliance necessity. The result is a growing attack surface. In late 2025, a single unsecured database belonging to the verification provider IDMerit exposed approximately one billion personal records across 26 countries, and the financial sector saw cyber incidents more than double from 864 in 2024 to over 1,800 in 2025.


## The Data Minimization Gap


The mismatch between what compliance requires and what institutions collect is a data minimization problem.[Data minimization](https://blog.spruceid.com/zerotrust-what-is-data-minimization-and-why-does-it-matter-for-government-services/) is the principle that systems should collect and retain only the personal information that a specific purpose actually requires, and no more. It is foundational to privacy-by-design architecture and increasingly referenced in state and federal privacy guidance.


Most KYC workflows were designed before modern identity verification technology existed. A cryptographically verifiable claim from an authoritative source can now answer specific compliance questions without requiring the institution to receive and store the full document or attribute set. Closing the gap between what compliance requires and what institutions collect requires rethinking the architecture of the verification decision itself.


## How Verifiable digital credentials Change the Verification Model


A[verifiable digital credential](https://blog.spruceid.com/digitalidentity-how-do-verifiable-digital-credentials-work-a-non-technical-explanation/) is a cryptographically signed assertion issued by an authoritative party: a government agency, a licensed identity provider, or a regulated institution whose attestation carries trust. The credential binds claims about a subject to a digital signature that a relying party can verify without contacting the issuer in real time, and without necessarily receiving the full set of attributes the issuer holds.


In a KYC context, this means an institution can receive a credential that confirms a customer's verified identity without receiving the raw document the issuer used to confirm it. The government or identity provider that issued the credential has already performed the liveness check, the document authentication, and the identity proofing. The institution receives the outcome, cryptographically bound to the issuer's key, along with the specific attributes it needs for its compliance record.


This shifts who performs identity proofing. Under a traditional flow, the institution both collects the raw document and attempts to verify it. Under a verifiable digital credential model, the institution relies on verification that an authoritative party has already performed. That is a different risk allocation, and often a more defensible one: the institution can demonstrate reliance on an authoritative cryptographic attestation rather than its own visual assessment of a document copy.


## Selective Disclosure: Answering Compliance Questions Without Oversharing


[Selective disclosure](https://blog.spruceid.com/digitalidentity-what-is-selective-disclosure-and-how-do-verifiable-digital-credentials-reveal-only-whats-needed/) refers to the ability of a credential holder to present only a subset of the claims in a credential, chosen to answer a specific question, while the cryptographic integrity of the entire credential remains verifiable. Several credential formats support selective disclosure natively.[SD-JWT VC](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-oauth-sd-jwt-vc/?ref=blog.spruceid.com) , an IETF standard nearing final publication, replaces plaintext claims with cryptographic hashes so the holder chooses which claims to reveal. BBS signatures, currently progressing through the[IETF CFRG](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-irtf-cfrg-bbs-signatures/?ref=blog.spruceid.com) as an Internet-Draft, go further by enabling unlinkable proofs and zero-knowledge predicate checks. The[ISO/IEC 18013-5](https://www.iso.org/standard/69084.html?ref=blog.spruceid.com) mobile driver's license standard also supports selective attribute presentation at the protocol level. Selective disclosure is distinct from zero-knowledge proofs, though BBS signatures bridge the two: selective disclosure reveals specific claims from a credential, while ZKPs allow proving a statement about claims (such as "age is above 18") without revealing the underlying value.


Consider a CIP verification for a retail banking account. The institution needs to confirm the customer's name, date of birth, and address, and to document that verification. It does not necessarily need to know the customer's full Social Security number in order to satisfy that specific requirement in all contexts. Selective disclosure allows the customer to present the specific attributes from a verified credential without exposing everything the issuer holds. The verifier can confirm that the presented attributes came from a valid credential without receiving the full credential.


The practical effect is that institutions can satisfy specific compliance checks without building a comprehensive identity dossier on every customer. Each transaction or account-opening event becomes an exchange of exactly the information needed, rather than a bulk transfer of identity data that then accumulates in the institution's systems.


The benefit runs in both directions. Customers share less personal information than they would under a traditional collection flow. Institutions carry less liability, because data they do not hold cannot be breached, cannot be subpoenaed in excess of what the law requires, and cannot become a finding in a regulatory examination for over-collection.


## Zero-Knowledge Proofs for Threshold Compliance Checks


Some KYC and AML compliance checks reduce naturally to threshold questions. Is this customer on a sanctions list? Is their age above the required threshold for a specific product? Does their address fall within a jurisdiction that requires enhanced due diligence? These questions can, in principle, be answered with a yes or no, without requiring the institution to receive the underlying data that determines the answer.


Zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) allow a prover to demonstrate that a statement is true, such as "my age is above 18" or "I am not on this list," without revealing the underlying value. Applied to KYC, certain compliance checks could be satisfied with a cryptographic proof of the outcome rather than the personal data underlying it.


ZKP applications in financial services compliance are not yet standard practice. Neither FinCEN nor the OCC has issued formal guidance addressing whether ZKP-based verification satisfies examination requirements. Institutions exploring this approach will need to engage their regulatory supervisors directly. The regulatory conversation about acceptability is the bottleneck, not the underlying cryptography.


## BSA and AML Implications


The[BSA](https://www.fincen.gov/resources/statutes-and-regulations/bank-secrecy-act?ref=blog.spruceid.com) 's recordkeeping requirements, and the broader anti-money laundering (AML) framework established by FinCEN, introduce additional considerations beyond account-opening CIP. In April 2026, FinCEN issued a[notice of proposed rulemaking](https://www.fincen.gov/news/news-releases/fincen-proposes-rule-fundamentally-reform-financial-institution-programs?ref=blog.spruceid.com) to reform AML/CFT program requirements under the BSA, shifting toward an effectiveness-based, risk-driven framework. Notably, FinCEN's proposed rule explicitly encourages financial institutions to responsibly adopt innovative technologies, including digital identity tools, as part of their compliance programs.


A privacy-preserving identity architecture needs to account for the full AML lifecycle, not just onboarding. Reusable KYC credentials offer a relevant design pattern: if an institution can rely on a verified credential that persists across interactions and refreshes when attributes change, it maintains a verifiable chain of identity without repeated full re-collection. SpruceID has[explored how verifiable digital identity can modernize BSA and AML/CFT compliance](https://blog.spruceid.com/modernizing-bsa-and-aml-cft-compliance-with-verifiable-digital-identity/) in more technical detail.


Enhanced due diligence cases may still warrant traditional collection in some circumstances. Privacy-preserving approaches reduce the baseline collection for standard-risk customers, which is where the bulk of unnecessary retention accumulates.


## What Mobile Driver's Licenses Add to the Picture


Mobile driver's licenses (mDLs), issued under the ISO/IEC 18013-5 standard and increasingly accepted across U.S. state programs, represent a government-issued identity credential that institutions can verify today.[mDLs bring several properties to financial services identity verification](https://blog.spruceid.com/how-mobile-drivers-licenses-can-transform-identity-verification-in-financial-services/) that static document copies do not: they are cryptographically bound to the issuing DMV's key, they can be verified without connecting to the issuer in real time, and they support selective presentation of specific attributes.


An mDL presentation at account opening can satisfy the documentary verification requirement of the CIP rule while enabling the institution to receive only the attributes it needs. The DMV has already performed the identity proofing; the institution receives a verified result. This does not eliminate the institution's responsibility to maintain its own compliance records, but it strengthens the evidentiary basis for those records while reducing the data the institution needs to collect and retain.


The regulatory acceptance of mDL-based verification for CIP purposes is advancing. In June 2025, the FDIC, OCC, and NCUA, with FinCEN's concurrence, issued an exemption order modernizing CIP requirements to allow institutions to rely on trusted third parties for identity verification rather than collecting information directly from customers. NIST's National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence has published[draft practice guidelines (SP 1800-42A)](https://www.nccoe.nist.gov/news-insights/nist-guidelines-implementing-mobile-drivers-licenses-financial-institutions?ref=blog.spruceid.com) for financial institutions implementing mDLs for customer identity verification, developed in collaboration with 29 industry and government partners, addressing how mDLs can meet CIP compliance requirements. FinCEN has recognized that digital identity tools, including electronic credentials, are viable methods for identity verification under the CIP framework.


## Building the Compliance Record Without Over-Retaining the Source Data


A question that compliance officers reasonably raise about privacy-preserving approaches is: what do we produce on examination? The answer lies in what constitutes an adequate compliance record.


The CIP record requirement can be satisfied by documenting what verification was performed, through what method, and with what result. A record showing that an institution verified a customer's identity through a cryptographically signed credential from a licensed identity provider or DMV, with a log of the specific attributes confirmed and the timestamp of verification, satisfies the regulatory documentation requirement. The institution does not need to retain the raw credential, the source document the issuer used to create it, or the full attribute set from the issuer's records.


This is a design decision that requires legal and compliance review specific to each institution's regulatory relationships. The June 2025 interagency CIP exemption order and NIST's ongoing mDL-to-CIP mapping project both signal that regulators are actively engaging with modern verification approaches. Institutions that have engaged with their examiners about digital credential-based verification have generally found regulators more receptive than a conservative read of older guidance might suggest.


The underlying principle is the same[zero trust design principle](https://blog.spruceid.com/zerotrust-what-is-zero-trust-the-basics-explained/) applied to identity: verify rigorously, document the verification, and do not retain source materials that serve no ongoing compliance function.


## Where the Complexity Actually Lives


The technical standards for privacy-preserving KYC exist. The[W3C Verifiable Credentials Data Model 2.0](https://www.w3.org/TR/vc-data-model-2.0/?ref=blog.spruceid.com) , published as a W3C Recommendation in May 2025, provides the credential format framework. SD-JWT VC and BBS signatures provide selective disclosure mechanisms for different use cases. ISO/IEC 18013-5 governs mDL issuance and presentation. OpenID for Verifiable Presentations (OID4VP) provides a standard presentation protocol.


The complexity that remains is not primarily technical. It is concentrated in three areas.


Regulatory acceptance is uneven. Examination guidance has not kept pace with technical capability, and institutions face real uncertainty about whether a digital credential-based verification will be treated equivalently to a traditional documentary verification during an exam. Institutions that want to move ahead should engage their primary regulator directly and build detailed examination-ready documentation of their verification architecture.


Credential availability is still developing. Not all customers will have a credential that an institution can verify, particularly in early deployment phases. A privacy-preserving approach cannot be the only available verification pathway; it needs to coexist with traditional methods for customers who lack compatible credentials. Designing a hybrid workflow that treats credential-based verification as the preferred path while maintaining a documentary fallback is operationally straightforward, but it requires explicit design rather than happening by default.


Vendor claims in this space require scrutiny. Several identity verification providers have attached "privacy-preserving" language to products that still accumulate significant personal data on the provider's infrastructure. The relevant question is not whether a product uses verifiable digital credentials in some form, but whether the end-to-end data flow actually minimizes collection at the institution level. Institutions should examine where data lands, who retains it, and under what contractual conditions, rather than accepting a vendor's architectural description at face value.


## A Practical Starting Point


Institutions do not need to replace their entire verification infrastructure to begin. A useful starting point is auditing current data retention against compliance necessity: for each category of identity data collected at onboarding, ask what compliance purpose it serves and what would be required to document that purpose without the raw data.


That audit typically surfaces significant room for reduction before any new technology is deployed. Addressing over-retention, designing tighter collection scopes for new accounts, and evaluating digital credential verification for certain customer segments are separable work streams that can be sequenced based on regulatory readiness.


Institutions that audit retention practices now, engage their regulators on modern verification methods, and build hybrid workflows with clear documentation will be better positioned than those who treat the current model as the default indefinitely.
